extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy and informed public (late-18th-century political audience)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political essay reflecting on the French Revolution, arguing principles about rights, government, and prudence in political reform. The text offers normative standards for constructing and judging governments and revolutionary conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: No man should be judge in his own cause
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the first motives to civil society ... that no man should be judge in his own cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By this each person divests himself of the uncovenanted right to judge for himself and to assert his own cause; he abdicates being his own governor and largely abandons the right of self-defence. This is a foundational rule of civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government exists to provide for human wants
rubrics_metrics.description: Government is a contrivance of human wisdom to provide for human wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural rights may exist independently, but government is practical and formed to supply wants (including restraint upon passions). Men have a right that these wants should be provided for by governmental wisdom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraints are part of citizens' rights
rubrics_metrics.description: The restraints on men, as well as their liberties, are to be reckoned among their rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because liberties and restrictions vary with time and circumstance, they cannot be settled by abstract rules; restraint by an external power is required to subject passions of individuals and the mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional design is a practical art requiring experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution of a state, and the due distribution of its powers, is a matter of the most delicate and complicated skill requiring deep knowledge of human nature and necessities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The science of constructing or reforming a commonwealth is not to be taught a priori; it requires long experience. One should be cautious about pulling down institutions that have functioned tolerably for ages, and should prefer models of approved utility when building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid applying metaphysical abstract rights as political rules
rubrics_metrics.description: These metaphysic rights entering into common life ... are, by the laws of Nature, refracted from their straight line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In complex human affairs primitive rights undergo such variety of refractions that it is absurd to treat them as if they continued in original simplicity. Political arrangements must accommodate complexity, not abstract principles alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple governments are fundamentally defective
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple governments are fundamentally defective ... If you contemplate society in but one point of view, simple modes of polity are captivating but inadequate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex forms, though imperfect, are preferable because they attempt to answer multiple, sometimes conflicting, ends rather than perfectly serving only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political rights are compromises and use practical calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights of men in governments are their advantages; these are often balances between differences of good — in compromises between good and evil, and sometimes between evil and evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political reason functions as a computing principle — adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing morally — rather than following metaphysical or mathematical absolutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish right from power; rights constrained by prudence and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: By these theorists the right of the people is almost always sophistically confounded with their power ... Men have no right to what is not reasonable, and to what is not for their benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Until power and right are the same, popular power cannot claim rights inconsistent with virtue and prudence; imprudent claims are not rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against constant rhetoric of resistance and revolution
rubrics_metrics.description: I never liked this continual talk of resistance and revolution ... It renders the habit of society dangerously valetudinary; it relaxes and wears out the spring of that spirit which is to be exerted on great occasions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overuse of revolutionary medicine makes society habitually sick and weakens capacity for genuine resistance when necessary; periodic enthusiasm or rhetoric of revolution is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorists of extremes are politically harmful and hypocritical
rubrics_metrics.description: The pretended rights of these theorists are all extremes ... these professors, finding their extreme principles not applicable, often employ no resistance at all or abandon public principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such theorists alternate between extremes to suit designs, exhibit hypocrisy, and often abandon practical virtue when theory proves inconvenient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutionary assemblies under coercion cannot deliberate freely
rubrics_metrics.description: With a compelled appearance of deliberation, they vote under the dominion of a stern necessity ... It is notorious that all their measures are decided before they are debated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemblies surrounded by armed force or mobs make decisions under terror; such 'deliberation' lacks liberty and impartiality and yields measures suggested by clubs and mobs rather than sober debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public clubs and academies that valorize violence deform policy
rubrics_metrics.description: In these meetings ... every counsel, in proportion as it is daring and violent and perfidious, is taken for the mark of superior genius. Humanity and compassion are ridiculed as the fruits of superstition and ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When daring violence is idolized in public fora, policy becomes monstrous: assassination, massacre, confiscation follow and virtue is driven to destitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not celebrate or sanctify violent triumphs
rubrics_metrics.description: I find a preacher of the Gospel profaning ... applying 'Nunc dimittis' to the most horrid, atrocious, and afflicting spectacle ... 'leading in triumph' a thing in its best form unmanly and irreligious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious or civic rites should not be used to consecrate scenes of massacre or atrocity; praising or commemorating violent deeds is morally shocking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware utilitarian justification of homicide if the people 'gain'
rubrics_metrics.description: On the scheme of this barbarous philosophy ... The murder of a king, or a queen, or a bishop, or a father, are only common homicide — and if the people are by any chance or in any way gainers by it, a sort of homicide much the most pardonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating regicide or parricide as excusable if politically advantageous undermines law, affection, and civilized sentiment; laws supported only by terror cannot engender veneration or attachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public affections and manners are necessary supplements to law
rubrics_metrics.description: These public affections, combined with manners, are required sometimes as supplements, sometimes as correctives, always as aids to law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reason that banishes affections cannot fill their place; institutions must be embodied in persons and supported by social sentiments like honor, courtesy, and attachment, not only by mechanical law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise prudence when praising 'new light' or rapid social change
rubrics_metrics.description: Before I proceed further, I have to remark that Dr. Price seems rather to overvalue the great acquisitions of light which he has obtained and diffused in this age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of unique discovery of political 'light' or superiority to previous ages should be treated skeptically; historical precedents often show similar claims and unintended consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not dismantle institutions without proven models of utility
rubrics_metrics.description: It is with infinite caution that any man ought to venture upon pulling down an edifice which has answered in any tolerable degree for ages the common purposes of society, or on building it up again without having models and patterns of approved utility before his eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should rely on experience and proven examples rather than abstract theorizing when undertaking major institutional changes.
